title: Visiting a temple
hookLine: shoes off, bow, sit toward the back, don't point your feet at the shrine

lines: A PILE OF SHOES BY THE STEPS.
WHAT IF I DO IT WRONG?
cards: You're standing at the gate of a temple for the first time. There's a pile of shoes by the steps. Inside, a soft chant, and the smell of incense.
Someone walks past you and bows. First-time visitors tend to carry the questions of a guest at a stranger's wedding: am I dressed right, where do I stand, what if I do it wrong?
A handful of customs covers most of it, and a guest who's trying is usually met kindly.

teach.b: Shoes off. At the door of the shrine hall, and in some countries at the gate of the whole temple, shoes come off; look for the pile and add yours. Dress simply, with shoulders and knees covered.

Inside, many Buddhists bow three times, the three bows from your very first week, to the Buddha, the teaching and the community. In Theravada temples it's often a five-point bow: forehead, forearms and knees to the floor.

As a guest, you can simply put your palms together at your chest and lower your head a little. That gesture is anjali; in Thailand it's the wai. Sit toward the back, on the floor or a chair, whatever others are doing.

teach.h: SIT BACK, FEET AWAY FROM THE SHRINE.
teach.b: And the custom that's easiest to miss: don't point your feet at the Buddha image, the shrine, or a monk. In much of Asia the feet are the lowest part of the body, so pointing them is like pointing a dirty shoe.

Sit cross-legged, or fold your legs to the side. A few more. In many Theravada temples, women don't touch monks or hand them things directly; an offering is placed on a cloth or passed through someone else.
Walk clockwise around a stupa. Ask before taking photos. Don't touch or climb on images.
Customs differ between a Thai temple, a Japanese one and a Tibetan one; when in doubt, watch and copy, or ask. Now look back at the week. Carried into exile.
In between. The diamond day. You need people.
The whole of the path. Test it yourself.

how: Visitors to Buddhist temples usually remove their shoes, dress modestly, bow or join their palms, sit toward the back and keep their feet from pointing at the shrine or monks; in many Theravada temples women do not hand things directly to monks.

o: an offering of flowers at the shrine
a full bow with forehead to the floor
palms joined at the chest in respect

games.q: match each temple custom with its reason.
p: at the door of the shrine hall
the feet are the lowest part

s: it's fine to stretch your legs out toward the Buddha image
keep your feet from pointing at the Buddha image, the shrine or a monk; fold your legs to the side.
in many Theravada temples, women don't hand things directly to monks
an offering is placed on a cloth or passed through someone else.
you must know every custom before your first visit
when in doubt, watch and copy, or ask; people are usually gracious to guests.

games.q: you're sitting in a Thai temple and your legs are cramping. what's the respectful way to shift?
o: stretch them straight out toward the shrine.
fold them to the side, feet pointing away.
stand up and walk around the hall.
games.why: fold your legs to the side, with your feet pointing away from the Buddha image and the monks.

practice: Picture yourself at a temple gate, even for a visit months away: shoes off, palms together, a seat toward the back, feet tucked away from the shrine. Notice how the nerves feel, and let them be.
Then sit here the way you'd sit there: quietly, a guest in a room full of other people's devotion.

wordCard.voice: Anjali. The gesture of palms joined at the chest, a greeting and a sign of respect used when entering a shrine hall.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit añjali: the gesture of palms joined at the chest, a greeting and a sign of respect.

carryVoice: Your line: shoes off. A handful of customs, and a guest who's trying. A week done; see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Temple etiquette across Theravada, Mahayana and Tibetan communities (living practice)
